title: Temurah 7
description: Where Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, finds a prohibition on collecting the blood of a blemished offering, whether one who consecrates an animal blemished from birth is flogged, blemished animals for Temple maintenance, Abaye refuted on the general prohibition, and the mishna on priests who substitute for offerings they received.
topics: 🩸 Collecting the blood: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, and the three phrases of Leviticus 22, in two versions
🌴 Blemished from birth: “a mere date palm”, or a disgraceful matter?
🍷 Rava: even consecrating it for the value of libations brings lashes
🏛️ “You may offer it for a gift”: blemished animals for Temple maintenance, unblemished ones not
🗣️ “Lemor”: “No is stated”, from Rabbi and bar Kappara
⚖️ Abaye and the general prohibition: all of it, part of it, and a conclusive refutation
🐑 Priests substitute for their own offerings, but not for a sin offering, a guilt offering or a firstborn
💰 Selling a firstborn unblemished and alive: only nowadays?

a1.he: סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: בִּשְׁלָמָא מֵעִיקָּרָא לָא יָדַעְנָא אִי הַאי מִיקְּבַע לַשֵּׁם, אֲבָל הָכָא, כֵּיוָן דְּאִינְּכַר שֵׁם — לָא לָקֵי, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

a2.he: אָמַר מָר: מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַף קַבָּלַת הַדָּם. מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה? אָמַר קְרָא: ״וּמָעוּךְ וְכָתוּת וְנָתוּק וְכָרוּת וְגוֹ׳״ — זוֹ קַבָּלַת הַדָּם, שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.

a3.he: וּלְתַנָּא קַמָּא, הַאי ״לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ״ לְמָה לִי? מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לִזְרִיקַת דָּמִים. וְהָא נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵ״עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״? אוֹרְחֵיהּ דִּקְרָא דְּמִשְׁתַּעֵי הָכִי.

a4.he: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה נָמֵי, אוֹרְחֵיהּ דִּקְרָא הוּא? אִין הָכִי נָמֵי. אֶלָּא קַבָּלַת הַדָּם מְנָא לֵיהּ? נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵהָא: ״וּמִיַּד בֶּן נֵכָר לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ״ — זוֹ הִיא קַבָּלַת הַדָּם שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.

a5.he: וּלְתַנָּא קַמָּא, הַאי ״לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ״ לְמָה לִי? מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְהַאי: סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא, הוֹאִיל וְלֹא נִצְטַוּוּ בְּנֵי נֹחַ אֶלָּא עַל מְחוּסַּר אֵבָרִים, לָא שְׁנָא בְּמִזְבֵּחַ דִּידְהוּ וְלָא שְׁנָא בְּמִזְבֵּחַ דִּידַן, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

a6.he: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל קַבָּלַת הַדָּם. מַאי טַעְמָא? דִּכְתִיב: ״וּמָעוּךְ וְכָתוּת... לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ״ — זוֹ קַבָּלַת הַדָּם, וּזְרִיקָה נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵ״עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״.

a7.he: וּלְרַבָּנַן נָמֵי תִּיפּוֹק לְהוּ זְרִיקָה מִן ״עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״! הָכִי נָמֵי, וְאֶלָּא ״לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ״ דְּמָעוּךְ לְמַאי אֲתָא? מַפְּקִינַן [לֵיהּ] לְבָמַת יָחִיד.

a8.he: וּלְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, הַאי מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְבָמַת יָחִיד? אִין הָכִי נָמֵי, אֶלָּא ״תַּקְרִיבוּ״ דְּקַבָּלָה מְנָא לֵיהּ? ״מִיָּד בֶּן נֵכָר לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ״ — זוֹ קַבָּלַת הַדָּם.

a9.he: וְרַבָּנַן אִצְטְרִיךְ, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: הוֹאִיל וּבְנֵי נֹחַ אֵין מְצוִּּוין אֶלָּא עַל מְחוּסַּר אֵבֶר בְּבָמָה דִּלְהוֹן, דִּלְמָא אֲנַן נָמֵי נְקַבֵּיל מִינְּהוֹן? קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן ״מִכׇּל אֵלֶּה״ דְּלָא מְקַבְּלִינַן.

a10.he: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: שֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁנִינוּ אֶלָּא בְּתָם שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה בַּעַל מוּם, וְעוֹבֵר, דְּאִי בַּעַל מוּם מֵעִיקָּרָא — דִּיקְלָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא!

a11.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף: ״שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט״ כְּתִיב בַּפָּרָשָׁה, וְהָנֵי בַּעֲלֵי מוּמִין מֵעִיקָּרָא נִינְהוּ.

a12.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁנִינוּ אֶלָּא בִּתְמוּרָה, דִּתְנַן: חוֹמֶר בַּתְּמוּרָה מִבַּזֶּבַח, שֶׁכֵּן קְדוּשָּׁה חָלָה עָלֶיהָ עַל בַּעַל מוּם קָבוּעַ.

a13.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לָא שְׁמִיעַ לָךְ הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי, בַּחֲבוּרָה נִמְנוּ וְגָמְרוּ: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ בַּעַל מוּם לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ עוֹבֵר מִשּׁוּם חֲמִשָּׁה שֵׁמוֹת, וְאִי בִּתְמוּרָה נָמֵי — שִׁשָּׁה הָוְויָין, דְּאִיכָּא נָמֵי לָאו דִּתְמוּרָה! אֶלָּא מַאי — בְּבַעַל מוּם מֵעִיקָּרוֹ? אַמַּאי לָקֵי? דִּיקְלָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא!

a14.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּיקְלָא — לָאו זִילָא מִילְּתָא, מִין עֵצִים הוּא; בַּעַל מוּם מֵעִיקָּרָא — זִילָא מִילְּתָא, כֵּיוָן דִּשְׁבֵיק תְּמִימִים וְאַקְדֵּישׁ בַּעֲלֵי מוּמִין — מִיחַיַּיב.

a15.he: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲפִילּוּ הָכִי בַּזְיָא מִילְּתָא, דְּדֶקֶל לֵיכָּא בְּמִינוֹ — לָא לָקֵי, לְאַפּוֹקֵי בַּעַל מוּם, כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא בְּמִינוֹ — לָקֵי.

a16.he: אָמַר רָבָא: הַשְׁתָּא דַּאֲמוּר טַעְמָא דְּבַעַל מוּם דְּלָקֵי — מִשּׁוּם דְּבַזְיָא מִילְּתַיְיהוּ, אֲפִילּוּ (למקדיש) [מַקְדֵּישׁ] לֵיהּ לִדְמֵי נְסָכִים — נָמֵי לָקֵי.

b1.he: ״נְדָבָה תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתוֹ״ — זֶה קׇדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת, וְאֵין לִי אֶלָּא נְדָבָה, נֶדֶר מִנַּיִן? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״וּלְנֵדֶר״.

b2.he: יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ קׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״וּלְנֵדֶר לֹא יֵרָצֶה״, זֶה קׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ. וְאֵין לִי אֶלָּא נֶדֶר, נְדָבָה מִנַּיִן? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״נְדָבָה״. רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: ״לֹא יֵרָצֶה״ — בְּהַרְצָאַת גּוּפוֹ הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר.

b3.he: הַיְינוּ תַּנָּא קַמָּא! מַאי לָאו בְּהָא קָמִיפַּלְגִי, דְּתַנָּא קַמָּא סָבַר: אֲפִילּוּ אַקְדְּשֵׁיהּ לִדְמֵי נְסָכִים — נָמֵי לָקֵי, וְרַבִּי סָבַר: בְּהַרְצָאַת גּוּפוֹ — נָמֵי לָקֵי, אֲבָל בִּדְמֵי נְסָכִים — לָא לָקֵי. שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ.

b4.he: וְאֶלָּא ״אוֹתוֹ״ לְמָה לִי? לְכִדְתַנְיָא: ״נְדָבָה תַּעֲשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ״ — ״אוֹתוֹ״ תַּעֲשֶׂה נְדָבָה, וְאִי אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה תָּמִים נְדָבָה לְבֶדֶק הַבַּיִת. מִיכָּן אָמְרוּ: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ תְּמִימִים לְבֶדֶק הַבַּיִת — עוֹבֵר בַּעֲשֵׂה.

b5.he: וּמִנַּיִן אַף בְּלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה — שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וַיְדַבֵּר ה׳ אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר״ — לִימֵּד עַל הַפָּרָשָׁה שֶׁהִיא בְּלָאו, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה.

b6.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי לְבַר קַפָּרָא: מַאי מַשְׁמַע? אֲמַר לֵיהּ דִּכְתִיב ״לֵאמֹר״ — ״לֹא״ נֶאֱמַר בַּדְּבָרִים. בֵּי רַבִּי אָמְרִי: ״לֹא אֱמוֹר״.

b7.he: אִיתְּמַר: הַמַּעֲלֶה אֵבְרֵי בַּעֲלֵי מוּמִין לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ, אָמַר רָבָא: עוֹבֵר מִשּׁוּם ״בַּל תַּקְטִירוּ כּוּלּוֹ״ וּמִשּׁוּם ״בַּל תַּקְטִירוּ מִקְצָתוֹ״. אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אֵין לוֹקִין עַל לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת.

b8.he: מֵיתִיבִי: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ בַּעֲלֵי מוּמִין לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ — עוֹבֵר מִשּׁוּם חֲמִשָּׁה שֵׁמוֹת, תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּאַבָּיֵי.

b9.he: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: בְּגַבְרֵי קָתָנֵי! אִי בְּגַבְרֵי — ״עוֹבֵר״?! ״עוֹבְרִין״ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ! אֶלָּא פְּשִׁיטָא בְּחַד גַּבְרָא, וּתְיוּבְתָּא דְאַבָּיֵי.

b10.he: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אַפֵּיק ״הַקְטָרַת מִקְצָתוֹ״, וְעַיֵּיל ״קַבָּלַת הַדָּם״. קַבָּלַת דָּם — לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אִית לֵיהּ, לְתַנָּא קַמָּא לֵית לֵיהּ? קַשְׁיָא!

b11.he: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: וְהָא מִדְּסֵיפָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא, רֵישָׁא רַבָּנַן. תְּיוּבְתָּא דְאַבָּיֵי, תְּיוּבְתָּא.

b12.he: מַתְנִי׳ הַכֹּהֲנִים מְמִירִין בְּשֶׁלָּהֶן, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל מְמִירִין בְּשֶׁלָּהֶן. אֵין הַכֹּהֲנִים מְמִירִין לֹא בְּחַטָּאת וְלֹא בְּאָשָׁם וְלֹא בִּבְכוֹר. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן נוּרִי: מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין מְמִירִין בִּבְכוֹר? אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם מַתָּנָה לַכֹּהֵן, וּבְכוֹר מַתָּנָה לַכֹּהֵן. מָה חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם אֵין מְמִירִין בּוֹ, אַף בְּכוֹר אֵין מְמִירִין בּוֹ.

b13.he: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן נוּרִי: מָה לוֹ אִם אֵינוֹ מֵמִיר בְּחַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם, שֶׁאֵין זָכִין בָּהֶן בְּחַיֵּיהֶן, תֹּאמַר בִּבְכוֹר שֶׁזָּכִין בּוֹ בְּחַיָּיו! אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר ״וְהָיָה הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ יִהְיֶה קּוֹדֶשׁ״, הֵיכָן קְדוּשָּׁה חָלָה עָלָיו? בְּבֵית הַבְּעָלִים, אַף תְּמוּרָה בְּבֵית הַבְּעָלִים.

b14.he: גְּמָ׳ תְּנַן הָתָם: בְּכוֹר מוֹכְרִין אוֹתוֹ תָּם חַי, וּבַעַל מוּם חַי וְשָׁחוּט, וּמְקַדְּשִׁין בּוֹ הָאִשָּׁה. אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה, הוֹאִיל וְאִית לֵיהּ לְכֹהֵן זְכִיָּיה בְּגַוֵּויהּ (הוֹאִיל וְיֵשׁ לַכֹּהֵן שׁוּתָּפוּת בּוֹ), אֲבָל בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים, כֵּיוָן דְּתָם לְהַקְרָבָה הוּא דְּקָאֵי — אֵין מוֹכְרִין אוֹתוֹ תָּמִים חַי.

b15.he: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב נַחְמָן: מוֹכְרִין אוֹתוֹ תָּמִים חַי — חַי אִין, שָׁחוּט לָא. אֵימַת? אִילֵּימָא בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה — מִי אִיכָּא תָּם שָׁחוּט? אֶלָּא פְּשִׁיטָא בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים, וְקָתָנֵי נָמֵי: מוֹכְרִין אוֹתוֹ תָּמִים חַי, (אַלְמָא אִית לֵיהּ לְכֹהֵן זְכִיָּיה בְּגַוֵּויהּ)!

b16.he: לָא, לְעוֹלָם בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה, מִי קָתָנֵי: מוֹכְרִין אוֹתוֹ תָּמִים חַי — אִין, שָׁחוּט — לָא? הִא גּוּפַאּ אֲתָא לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן, דְּבִזְמַן הַזֶּה נָמֵי מוֹכְרִין אוֹתוֹ תָּמִים חַי.

messages.text: 7a

Continued from 6b: the baraita derived from “unto the Lord” that a blemished animal may not serve as the scapegoat, and Rava explained that the verse is needed where the scapegoat became blemished on Yom Kippur itself and its sanctity was transferred onto another goat. His explanation continues.

Since it might enter your mind to say that granted, if one does this initially, before the lottery, we do not know if this blemished animal will be designated as the one sacrificed to the Lord or sent to the wilderness. Therefore, the one who consecrated the blemished animal is flogged.

notes.he: בעינן תמימין משום דלא ידענא אי האי מיקבע לשם אי האי מיקבע לשם כו':
notes.en: It might enter your mind to say: granted at the outset [before the lottery], we require unblemished animals, because I do not know whether this one will be fixed for the Name or that one will be fixed for the Name, etc.

messages.text: But here, since it is already clear that the other animal is to be sacrificed to the Lord, and the one he consecrates will be sent to the wilderness, perhaps he is not flogged for consecrating it. The verse therefore teaches us that this is also a violation of the prohibition and he is flogged.

notes.he: ל"א והא אין הגורל קובע כו' אמר רב יוסף הא מני חנן המצרי היא דלא בעי הגרלה דתניא חנן המצרי אומר אפי' דמו של שעיר הנעשה בפנים בכוס ומת כלומר שכבר נשחט ומת שעיר המשתלח מביא חבירו מביא שעיר אחר מן השוק ומזווג לו ומעמידו אצל הדם להראות שחבירו הוא ואחר כך משלחו אלמא לא בעי הגרלה וליכא למפרך הא דפרכינן הלכך איצטריך קרא:
notes.en: Another version [of the discussion at the end of 6b]: “But the lottery fixes only…” Rav Yosef said: Whose view is this? It is Ḥanan the Egyptian, who does not require a lottery, as it is taught: Ḥanan the Egyptian says: Even if the blood of the goat offered inside is in the cup and [the scapegoat] died, that is, [the inner goat] was already slaughtered and the scapegoat died, he brings its fellow: he brings another goat from the market, pairs it with it and stands it beside the blood, to show that it is its fellow, and afterward sends it away. Evidently he does not require a lottery, and the challenge we raised cannot be raised; therefore the verse was needed.

notes.dh: וקפריך אימור דשמעת ליה לחנן דלית ליה דחויין
notes.he: דלא יביא שנים אחרים ויגריל וישחוט האחד לשם והאחר לעזאזל והראשון שכבר נשחט ידחה וישפך דמו לאיבוד דלית ליה הגרלה מי שמעת ליה דלמא לעולם יביא שנים מן השוק ויגריל ואותו שיפול עליו הגורל לעזאזל יעמד עם דם שבכוס וישלחנו והדם שבכוס מזה ממנו כמשפטו ואותו שנפל עליו הגורל לשם ירעה עד שיסתאב. הא מני דמצריך קרא לרבות שעיר דלא ליהוי בעל מום רבי שמעון הוא דלית ליה הגרלה והכי הוי מסקנא ותו לא פריך מידי. והגירסא אימור דשמעת ליה לרבי שמעון כו' שבשתא היא דהא במסכת יומא (דף סג:) תנינן לה לכולה סוגיא ולא פרכינן התם מידי בפרק שני שעירי:
notes.en: And he challenges: Say that you heard of Ḥanan that he does not hold of deferral, that is, that one does not bring two other goats, draw lots, slaughter one for the Name and send the other to Azazel, while the first, already slaughtered, is deferred and its blood poured out to waste. But did you hear from him that he does not hold of a lottery? Perhaps he actually brings two from the market and draws lots; the one on which the lot for Azazel falls is stood beside the blood in the cup and sent away, the blood in the cup is sprinkled according to its law, and the one on which the lot for the Name fell grazes until it becomes blemished. Rather, whose view is it, that requires a verse to include the goat so that it may not be blemished? It is Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold of a lottery. This is the conclusion, and nothing further is challenged. The reading “Say that you heard of Rabbi Shimon, etc.” is an error, for in tractate Yoma (63b), in the chapter Shnei Se’irei, we learn this whole discussion and nothing is challenged there.

notes.he: כדפרישית לעיל (והא דגרסינן הכא) דכרעיה דראשון הוא ותירוצא דמתרץ כגון שהיה לו [חולה] בתוך ביתו כו' ל"ג ליה ושבשתא הוא דלא איירי הכא במחוסר זמן כלל אבל במסכת יומא (שם) תנינן לה בההיא סוגיא [רומייא] דמחוסר זמן היא והא ליכא למימר אם אינו עניין לבעל מום תנהו עניין למחוסר זמן דהא נפקא לן מחוסר זמן בשעיר המשתלח מלה' דאידך קרא ומיום השמיני והלאה וגו' מהכא נפקא במסכת יומא[ס"ג:]:
notes.en: Rava said: For example, where it became blemished, etc.: as I explained above, this is part of the first [answer]. The answer that reads “for example, where he had a sick person in his house, etc.” we do not read here; it is an error, for here the discussion does not deal with an animal lacking time at all. But in tractate Yoma (ibid.) we learn it in that discussion, where there is a contradiction concerning an animal lacking time. Here one cannot say “if it is not needed for a blemished animal, apply it to one lacking time,” for we derive lacking time for the scapegoat from “unto the Lord” of the other verse, “and from the eighth day onward”; it is from here that it is derived in tractate Yoma (63b).

messages.text: The Sages said in the name of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda: One who sacrifices a blemished animal violates a prohibition against the collection of the blood as well.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda?
messages.quote: the collection of the blood as well

messages.text: The verse states: “That which has its testicles bruised, or crushed, or torn, or cut, you shall not offer unto the Lord” (Leviticus 22:24). The phrase “You shall not offer unto the Lord” is apparently superfluous, as the Torah already stated earlier: “But whatever has a blemish, you shall not offer” (Leviticus 22:20). Rather, this extra phrase is referring to the collection of the blood, for which Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, said that one is liable.

verse.he: וּמָעוּךְ וְכָתוּת וְנָתוּק וְכָרוּת לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ לַיהֹוָה וּבְאַרְצְכֶם לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ׃
verse.en: You shall not offer to GOD anything [with its testes] bruised or crushed or torn or cut. You shall have no such practices in your own land,

messages.text: And according to the first tanna, who holds that one is not liable for collection of the blood per se, why do I need this phrase: “You shall not offer,” stated with regard to damaged testicles?
He requires it to teach that one is liable for sprinkling the blood.
But he derives this from the phrase: “Upon the altar” (Leviticus 22:22), which indicates that one may not sacrifice any part of such an animal on the altar, even its blood.

verse.he: עַוֶּרֶת אוֹ שָׁבוּר אוֹ־חָרוּץ אוֹ־יַבֶּלֶת אוֹ גָרָב אוֹ יַלֶּפֶת לֹא־תַקְרִיבוּ אֵלֶּה לַיהֹוָה וְאִשֶּׁה לֹא־תִתְּנוּ מֵהֶם עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Anything blind, or injured, or maimed, or with a wen, boil-scar, or scurvy—such you shall not offer to GOD; you shall not put any of them on the altar as offerings by fire to GOD.

messages.text: With regard to that phrase, the first tanna holds that it is simply the normal manner of the verse that it speaks like this. It does not teach any additional halakha.

notes.dh: אמר מר ר' יוסי בר' יהודה אמר אף על קבלת הדם כו'
notes.he: אורחיה דקרא דמשתעי הכי ע"ג המזבח ולאו לדרשא אתי אלא דלא תקריבו אתא:
notes.en: The Master said: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says: also for the collection of the blood, etc. [According to the first tanna,] “upon the altar” is the manner of the verse to speak thus and does not come for exposition; rather, “you shall not offer” comes [for sprinkling].

messages.text: But also according to Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, one may claim that this is the normal manner of the verse. Why does he derive a halakha from this phrase?
Yes, it is indeed so. He does not derive liability for sprinkling of the blood from the phrase “upon the altar.”

notes.dh: ור' יוסי בר' יהודה נמי אורחיה דקרא הוא
notes.he: ולאו לדרשא אתי והאי לא תקריבו מיבעי לזריקת דמים:
notes.en: And for Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, too, it is the manner of the verse and does not come for exposition, and this “you shall not offer” is needed for the sprinkling of the blood.

messages.text: Rather, from where does he derive the prohibition against collection of the blood? He derives it from this verse: “Neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer the bread of your God of any of these, because their corruption is in them; there is a blemish in them; they shall not be accepted for you” (Leviticus 22:25). This verse is referring to the collection of the blood when sacrificing a blemished animal, for which Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, said that one is liable.

verse.he: וּמִיַּד בֶּן־נֵכָר לֹא תַקְרִיבוּ אֶת־לֶחֶם אֱלֹהֵיכֶם מִכׇּל־אֵלֶּה כִּי מׇשְׁחָתָם בָּהֶם מוּם בָּם לֹא יֵרָצוּ לָכֶם׃ {ס}
verse.en: nor shall you accept such [animals] from a foreigner for offering as food for your God, for they are mutilated, they have a defect; they shall not be accepted in your favor.

notes.dh: ומיד בן נכר לא תקריבו את אלה
notes.he: וא"ת למה לי איש איש לרבות בני נח שנודרין נדרים ונדבות כישראל (חולין דף יג:) תיפוק ליה מהאי קרא דמדקאמר לא תקריבו את אלה משמע אלה אי אתה מקריב אבל אתה מקריב תמימים אבל איפכא ליכא למיבעיא מיד בן נכר למה לי תיפוק ליה מאיש איש דהא איצטריך בן נכר להאי דרשא דהכא לא שנא במזבח דידהו ולא שנא במזבח דידן (לא אמרינן) אלא איש איש למה לי ותירץ רבינו שמשון בר אברהם דאיצטריך להך פלוגתא דרבי יוסי הגלילי ורבי עקיבא בפרק ואלו מנחות (מנחות עג:) מה תלמוד לומר לעולה פרט לנזירות רבי עקיבא אמר עולה אין לי אלא עולה ולא שאר קרבנות:
notes.en: “And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer… of any of these”: And if you ask: why do I need “any man” to include descendants of Noah, who vow vows and gift offerings like Israel (Ḥullin 13b)? Derive it from this verse, for since it says “you shall not offer these,” it implies: these you do not offer, but you do offer unblemished ones. The reverse question does not arise, why do I need “from the hand of a foreigner” when it could be derived from “any man,” since “foreigner” is needed for the exposition here: whether on their altar or on our altar. Rather, why do I need “any man”? Rabbeinu Shimshon bar Avraham answered that it is needed for the dispute of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva in the chapter Ve’elu Menaḥot (Menaḥot 73b): What does the verse teach by “for a burnt offering”? To exclude nazirite offerings; Rabbi Akiva says: “burnt offering”: I have only a burnt offering, not other offerings.

notes.dh: ואלא קבלת הדם מנא ליה נפקא ליה [מהא] ומיד בן נכר לא תקריבו
notes.he: לא נצטוו בני נח אלא על מחוסרי אברים דכתיב מכל החי [מכל בשר] הביא בהמה שחיין ראשי אברין שלה:
notes.en: But collection of the blood, from where does he derive it? He derives it from this: “And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer.” The descendants of Noah were commanded only regarding animals lacking limbs, as it is written: “Of every living thing of all flesh” (Genesis 6:19): bring an animal whose principal limbs are alive.

messages.text: And according to the first tanna, who holds that one is not liable for collection of the blood, why do I need this phrase: Neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer?

He requires it to teach this halakha: It may enter your mind to say that since the descendants of Noah are commanded only with regard to the sacrifice of an animal lacking limbs but they are permitted to sacrifice animals with minor blemishes, perhaps there is no difference if this is performed on their altar outside the Temple or if it is done on our altar in the Temple.

notes.he: בני נח נצטוו מלהקריב מחוסרי אברים כדאמרי' בפרק קמא דע"ז (דף ה:) אבל על מום אחר לא נצטוו במזבח דידהו. ואי לא כתיב לא תקריבו מאת בן נכר את כל אלה דמשמע בעל מום לא יקבלו מן העובד כוכבים להקריב הוה אמינא ליקרב אלא שלא יהו מחוסרי אברים קמ"ל:
notes.en: The descendants of Noah were commanded not to sacrifice animals lacking limbs, as we say in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (5b), but regarding any other blemish they were not commanded, on their own altar. And had it not been written “neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer… of any of these,” which implies that a blemished animal is not accepted from a gentile to be sacrificed, I would have said it may be offered, provided only that it is not lacking a limb. It teaches us [otherwise].

notes.he: במזבח דידן לישתרי לאיתויי קרבן דידהו בעל מום דלאו מחוסר אבר:
notes.en: It might enter your mind: on our altar it should be permitted to bring their offering that is blemished, but not lacking a limb.

messages.text: Accordingly, one might claim that a gentile may sacrifice a blemished animal in the Temple in Jerusalem. The verse therefore teaches us that they may not sacrifice a blemished animal in such a manner.

notes.he: בבמת יחיד שעשה העובד כוכבי' לשמים וקמ"ל מכל אלה דלא מקבלין כלומר להכי לא מקבלינן דהא כתיב בההוא קרא מכל אלה דמשמע לא תקבל בעל מום ה"נ לדידהו במזבח המיוחד:
notes.en: On their bama: on a private altar that the gentile made to Heaven. And it teaches us by “of any of these” that we do not accept: that is, this is why we do not accept it, since it is written in that verse “of any of these,” implying you shall not accept a blemished animal; so too for them, on the designated altar [in the Temple].

notes.he: מיד בן נכר לא תקריבו כו' מום בו [מכל] מום קבוע:
notes.en: It teaches us: “Neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer… there is a blemish in them”: [any] permanent blemish.

messages.text: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the discussion.
One violates a prohibition for the collection of the blood as well.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda?
messages.quote: for the collection of the blood as well

messages.text: As it is written: “That which has its testicles bruised, or crushed, or torn, or cut, you shall not offer unto the Lord” (Leviticus 22:24). This verse is referring to the collection of the blood. And he derives the prohibition against sprinkling the blood from the phrase: “Upon the altar” (Leviticus 22:22).
And according to the Rabbis as well, who hold that one is not liable for collection of the blood, let them derive liability for sprinkling the blood from the phrase “upon the altar.”

It is indeed so; they derive it from that phrase. But for what purpose comes the phrase “You shall not offer” with regard to bruised testicles? We learn from this phrase the prohibition of the sacrifice of a blemished animal even on a private altar, where offerings were sacrificed before the construction of the Temple.

notes.he: [מפקה ליה לבמת יחיד דאסור להקריב בה בעל מום]:
notes.en: [It excludes a private altar: it is prohibited to sacrifice a blemished animal on it.]

messages.text: But according to Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, how can he then derive the prohibition against collection of the blood of a blemished animal from the phrase “You shall not offer”? After all, he requires this phrase to render prohibited sacrifice on a private altar.

Yes, it is indeed so. Rather, where does he find another instance of the term “shall offer” for prohibiting collection of the blood? From the following verse: “Neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer the bread of your God of any of these, because their corruption is in them; there is a blemish in them; they shall not be accepted for you” (Leviticus 22:25). This verse is referring to the collection of the blood.

And the Rabbis maintain that this verse is necessary for a different halakha, as it may enter your mind to say that since the descendants of Noah are commanded only with regard to sacrificing an animal lacking a limb on their private altar but are permitted to sacrifice animals with minor blemishes, perhaps we should accept blemished offerings from them in the Temple as well.

notes.he: לאקרובי קרבנהון בבמה דילן בעל מום קבוע דלאו מחוסר אבר:
notes.en: We too should accept from them: to sacrifice their offering on our altar, blemished with a permanent blemish that is not a missing limb.

messages.text: Therefore, the verse teaches us by the use of the phrase “of any of these” that we do not accept them.

notes.he: מה אנן דומיא דמעוך וכתות דלאו מחוסר אבר אלא מום קבוע לא מקרבינן אף מנייהו לא נקביל:
notes.en: It teaches us “of any of these,” like us: just as for us, [blemishes] like bruised and crushed, which are not a missing limb but a permanent blemish, we do not sacrifice, so too from them we shall not accept.

messages.caption: Where each view ends up placing the three phrases of Leviticus 22, in both versions. In each version the Gemara first read 22:24 as Rabbi Yosei’s source for the collection of the blood, then moved that to 22:25.

messages.text: § The baraita cited earlier stated that one who consecrates a blemished animal violates several prohibitions, but it did not differentiate between animals born with blemishes and those that acquired them during their lives.

Perhaps we learned the prohibition only with regard to an unblemished animal that became blemished, and only one who consecrates such an animal transgresses the prohibition. As, if he consecrated an animal that was blemished from the outset, it is akin to consecrating a mere date palm, and his presumed intention is to consecrate its value, with the proceeds from its sale being used to purchase an offering. This would be permitted.

notes.he: לעיל קא מהדר דעובר בה' שמות שמא לא שנינו דילקה משום לא תקדישו אלא בתם ונעשה בעל מום משום דאיכא למימר הואיל ומעיקרא תם הוה סבר אע"פ שנפל בו מום אקדישנו ואקריבנו וכיון דלהקרבה מצינו [למימר] לאסוקי אדעתיה דאקדשיה לקי אבל בעל מום מעיקרא ממעי אמו דיקלא בעלמא הוא דאיכא למימר דלא אסיק אדעתיה [דחזי] לאקרוביה אלא לדמי אקדשיה ולא לקי:
notes.en: Reish Lakish objects: he is referring back to the statement above that one transgresses five prohibitions. Perhaps we learned that one is flogged for “you shall not consecrate” only with an unblemished animal that became blemished, for one can say: since it was unblemished at the outset, he thought, “Even though a blemish befell it, I will consecrate it and sacrifice it,” and since we can say he had sacrifice in mind when he consecrated it, he is flogged. But an animal blemished from the outset, from its mother’s womb, is a mere date palm, for one can say he did not have in mind that it was fit to be sacrificed but consecrated it only for its value, and he is not flogged.

notes.he: דאיכא למימר הואיל מעיקרא תם הוה סבר אע"פ שנפל בו מום אקדישנו ואקריבנו וכיון דלהקרבה מצינו [למימר] דאסוקי אדעתיה דאקדשינהו לילקי אבל בבעל מום מעיקרו ממעי אמו דיקלא בעלמא הוא ואיכא למימר דלא אסיק אדעתיה דחזי לאקרוביה לשון רש"י וקשה להר"ר מר היכי מצינו למימר דלא אסיק אדעתיה לאקרובי והלא התרו בו לא תקריב בעל מום למזבח והא קבל עליו התראה ואמר על מנת כן אני עושה דבלאו הכי לא לקי לכ"נ להר"ם לפרש דלא קאי ר"ש בן לקיש אבל תקדישו אלא אבל תקטירו ואבל תזריקו וה"פ לא שנו דעובר אבל תקטירו ואבל תזריקו אלא כשהקדישו תם ונעשה בעל מום דכיון דחלה עליו קדושת מזבח קודם שהומם אסיק אדעתיה דחזי להקרבה אבל בעל מום מעיקרו קודם קדושה דיקלא בעלמא הוא דלא מסיק אדעתיה דחזי להקרבה ולא לקי:
notes.en: Only with an unblemished animal that became blemished: for one can say that since it was unblemished at the outset, he thought, “Even though a blemish befell it, I will consecrate it and sacrifice it,” and since we can say he had sacrifice in mind when he consecrated it, he is flogged; but an animal blemished from the outset, from its mother’s womb, is a mere date palm, and one can say he did not have in mind that it was fit to be sacrificed. This is Rashi’s wording. Our teacher [the text reads הר״ר מר] found it difficult: how can we say he did not have sacrifice in mind, when they warned him, “Do not offer a blemished animal for the altar,” and he accepted the warning and said, “On that condition I am doing it”? Without that he is not flogged. Therefore the Maharam thought to explain that Reish Lakish refers not to “you shall not consecrate” but to “you shall not burn” and “you shall not sprinkle,” and this is the meaning: they taught that he transgresses “you shall not burn” and “you shall not sprinkle” only when he consecrated it unblemished and it became blemished, for since the sanctity of the altar took hold of it before it became blemished, he has in mind that it is fit to be sacrificed. But one blemished from the outset, before its consecration, is a mere date palm; he does not have in mind that it is fit to be sacrificed, and he is not flogged.

notes.dh: [מתקיף לה ריש לקיש] שמא לא שנינו כו'
notes.he: אברייתא קאי דקתני מיכן אמרו המקדיש בעלי מומין [למזבח עובר משום ה' לאוין וקאמר] שמא לא שנינו דלקי אלא בההוא דהוה תם מעיקרא [ונעשה בעל מום ולא בכל בעל מום דהיא בעל מום מעיקרא דההוא אמאי לקי דיקלא בעלמא הוא ליהוי כאילו הקדיש דיקלא בעלמא למזבח דלא כלום קאמר דלא הוה חזי ליה מעולם למזבח] ואמאי קתני בעל מום סתמא דמשמע נמי בעל מום מעיקרא:
notes.en: Reish Lakish objects: Perhaps we learned only, etc. He refers to the baraita that teaches: “From here they said: one who consecrates blemished animals for the altar transgresses five prohibitions.” And he says: perhaps we learned that one is flogged only for an animal that was unblemished at the outset and became blemished, and not for every blemished animal; for one that is blemished from the outset, why is he flogged? It is a mere date palm; let it be as though he consecrated a mere date palm for the altar, which is saying nothing, since it was never fit for the altar. And why does [the baraita] teach “blemished” without qualification, which implies also one blemished from the outset?

messages.text: @Reish Lakish The blemishes mentioned in the phrase in the verse that states: “Either a bull or a lamb that has anything too long or too short” (Leviticus 22:23), are written in the passage that prohibits the sacrifice of blemished animals, and animals such as these are blemished from the outset.

verse.he: וְשׁוֹר וָשֶׂה שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט נְדָבָה תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתוֹ וּלְנֵדֶר לֹא יֵרָצֶה׃
verse.en: You may, however, present as a freewill offering an ox or a sheep with a limb extended or contracted; but it will not be accepted for a vow.

notes.he: שנשתברה אחד מאבריו:
notes.en: Saru’a [too long]: one of whose limbs was broken [so the printed text; Rabbeinu Gershom, below, explains saru’a as one whose thigh is extended].

notes.he: שפרסותיו קלוטים:
notes.en: Kalut [too short]: whose hooves are uncloven.

notes.he: ועלייהו כתיב לא תקריבו ודרשינן לא תקדישו:
notes.en: Are written in the passage: and about them it is written “you shall not offer,” which we expound as “you shall not consecrate.”

notes.he: משום הכי קתני סתמא שרוע וקלוט כתובים בפרשה [דבעלי מומין] והני בעלי מומין מעיקרא נינהו [כדאמרן בפרק על אלו מומין שרוע שנשתרבבה ירכו. קלוט שרגליו קלוטות כשל חמור ושל סוס]:
notes.en: Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef said to him: this is why it teaches without qualification: saru’a and kalut are written in the passage of blemished animals, and these are blemished from the outset, as we said in the chapter Al Elu Mumin [Bekhorot 40b]: saru’a, whose thigh is extended; kalut, whose legs are uncloven like those of a donkey or a horse.

messages.text: Perhaps in the case of animals born with blemishes, we learned the prohibition only with regard to substitution, as we learned in a mishna (16b):
messages.lead: Reish Lakish said to Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef:

notes.he: שיהא חייב משום הקדשה אלא בתמורה לפי שהתמורה חלה על בעל מום קבוע וקדוש קדושה גמורה שאינה יוצאה לחולין ליגזז וליעבד אפילו על ידי פדיון אלא הויא כשאר קדשים שקדם הקדשן את מומן והך משנה לקמן בפרק שני (תמורה דף טז:) כדכתיב טוב ברע או רע בטוב ואם המר ימיר וגו' והואיל וקדושה גמורה היא לוקה עליה אם המיר והביא בעלת מום שיקדיש ותפסה בתמורת בהמת קודש תמימה אבל הקדיש בעל מום מעיקרא לא אמינא דלילקי דדיקלא בעלמא הוא אלא אם כן הקריבו:
notes.en: Perhaps we learned only: that one is liable for consecration only with substitution, for substitution takes effect on an animal with a permanent blemish, and it is fully sacred: it does not go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked even through redemption, but is like other consecrated animals whose consecration preceded their blemish. This mishna is below, in the second chapter (Temurah 16b), as it is written: “good for bad or bad for good, and if he shall substitute,” etc. And since it is full sanctity, he is flogged for it if he substituted, bringing a blemished animal to consecrate and it took effect as the substitute for an unblemished consecrated animal. But if he consecrated an animal blemished from the outset, I would not say he is flogged, for it is a mere date palm, unless he sacrificed it.

notes.he: שמא לא שנינו דלקי אלא בתמורה דהמיר בבעל מום:
notes.en: Perhaps we learned that one is flogged only with substitution, where he substituted with a blemished animal.

messages.text: There is greater stringency with regard to a substitute than there is with regard to the initial consecration of an offering, as, if one substituted a non-sacred animal with a permanent blemish for a consecrated unblemished animal, the blemished animal is imbued with sanctity.

notes.dh: דתנן חומר בתמורה מקדשים שהקדושה חלה עליה בבעל מום קבוע
notes.he: דכתיב לא ימיר אותו טוב ברע או רע בטוב היינו בעל מום וכתיב ואם המר ימירנו והיה הוא ותמורתו יהיה קדש וכיון דקדושה חלה עליה על בעל מום קבוע אינו יוצא לחולין ליגזז וליעבד מה שאין כן בשאר קדשים ששאר קדשים שקדם מום קבוע להקדישן יוצאין לחולין ליגזז וליעבד ושמא במקדיש בעל מום בתמורה קתני [ברייתא]:
notes.en: As we learned: there is greater stringency with substitution than with consecrated animals, in that sanctity takes hold of an animal with a permanent blemish, as it is written: “He shall not substitute it… good for bad or bad for good”; that is a blemished animal; and it is written: “And if he shall substitute… then both it and its substitute shall be sacred.” Since sanctity takes hold of it with a permanent blemish, it does not go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked, which is not so with other consecrated animals: other consecrated animals whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked. And perhaps the baraita teaches about one who consecrates a blemished animal through substitution.

messages.text: But initial consecration of an animal with such a blemish is effective only with regard to its value, so perhaps one who does so is exempt from punishment.

@Reish Lakish Didn’t you hear that which Rabbi Yannai says, that when the Sages sat in a group, their opinions were counted and they concluded: One who consecrates blemished animals for sacrifice on the altar violates five separate categories of prohibition.

notes.he: משמע שדקדקו ולא מצאו יותר. ואם איתא דעל ידי תמורה מישתעי:
notes.en: They were counted and concluded: this implies that they examined carefully and found no more. And if it were so that [the baraita] speaks of substitution,

messages.text: But if the baraita is also referring to a case of substitution, there are six categories, as there is also the prohibition of performing substitution.

notes.he: איכא לאו דלא ימיר:
notes.en: There would be six, for there is also the prohibition “he shall not substitute.”

messages.text: Rather, what can you say? Is the baraita speaking of one who consecrated an animal that is blemished from the outset? Why then is he flogged? It is akin to one who consecrates a mere date palm.

notes.he: ועל ידי הקדש אמאי לקי הא לא חיילא עליה קדושת מזבח כלל דדיקלא בעלמא הוא ולא אקדשיה אלא לדמי:
notes.en: Rather, what? With an animal blemished from the outset? And through consecration, why is he flogged? The sanctity of the altar does not take hold of it at all, for it is a mere date palm, and he consecrated it only for its value.

messages.text: There is a difference between the cases. When one consecrates a date palm, the matter is not disgraceful, as it is a type of wood that one may burn on the altar. Therefore, he is not flogged.
messages.quote: It is akin to one who consecrates a mere date palm

messages.text: By contrast, when one consecrates an animal that is blemished from the outset, the matter is disgraceful. Since he forsook unblemished animals and consecrated blemished animals, he is liable to be flogged.
The Gemara presents an alternative version of the previous point.

Nevertheless, the matter of consecrating an animal blemished from the outset is disgraceful. For in the case of a date palm, as there is no item of its type that can be sacrificed as an offering, he is not flogged for consecrating it. This is to the exclusion of a blemished animal; since there are items of its type that can be sacrificed as offerings, i.e., unblemished animals, he is flogged for consecrating it.

notes.he: הראוי למזבח:
notes.en: There is none of its kind: fit for the altar.

notes.he: ראוי למזבח וכיון דאיכא במינו ראוי איכא בזיון כיון דשבק מידי דחזי ואקדיש מידי דלא חזי:
notes.en: A blemished animal has [something] of its kind: fit for the altar. And since there is something of its kind that is fit, there is disgrace, since he left something fit and consecrated something unfit.

notes.he: דמקדיש בעל מום מעיקרו [מאוס טפי ממקדיש] דקל דמקדיש דקל לא הוי ביזוי דדקל ליכא במינו מובחר ממנו אבל בעל מום מעיקרא כיון דאיכא במינו ראוי ומקדיש בעל מום לקי [אפי' מקדיש ליה לדמי נסכים שיביאו בדמיו נסכים לקי]. [ואלא אותו למ"ל] כיון דקא דרשת הכי נדבה ולנדר ביחד ואלא אותו למאי אתיא לכדתניא כו':
notes.en: Even so, the matter is disgraceful: for one who consecrates an animal blemished from the outset [is more repugnant than one who consecrates] a date palm. One who consecrates a date palm causes no disgrace, for with a date palm there is nothing of its kind more choice than it. But an animal blemished from the outset: since there is something of its kind that is fit, and he consecrates a blemished one, he is flogged, [even if he consecrates it for the value of libations, so that libations are brought with its money, he is flogged]. [A marginal note here reads: “should read ‘in the mishna’.”] [Rather, why do I need “it”?] Since you expound “gift” and “vow” together, what does “it” come for? For that which is taught, etc.

messages.text: Now that it has been said that the reason that one who consecrates a blemished animal is flogged is due to the fact that the matter is disgraceful, then even one who consecrates it to be sold and its money used for purchasing libations should be flogged as well, as consecrating a blemished animal is in and of itself a disgraceful act.

notes.he: דהשתא ליכא בזיון כל כך שאין במינו ראוי לנסכים ועוד דהא לדמי אקדשיה אפי' הכי לקי:
notes.en: Even if he consecrated it for the value of libations: where there is now not so much disgrace, since nothing of its kind is fit for libations; and furthermore he consecrated it for its value. Even so, he is flogged.

notes.he: וה"ה מקדיש לדמי עולה והא דאמר לקמן (תמורה דף יח:) המקדיש נקבה לעולה ימכר ויפלו דמיו לעולה צ"ל דלקי וכן הא דתנן פרק כיצד מערימין (לקמן תמורה כז:) אמר על הבהמה טמאה ועל בעלת מום הרי אלו עולה לא אמר כלום הרי אלו לעולה ימכרו ויביא בדמיהם עולה צריך לומר דלקי:
notes.en: Even if he consecrated it for the value of libations he is flogged: and the same applies to one who consecrates it for the value of a burnt offering. And as for what is said below (Temurah 18b), that one who consecrates a female for a burnt offering, it is sold and its money goes for a burnt offering, one must say that he is flogged. Likewise what we learned in the chapter Keitzad Ma’arimin (below, Temurah 27b): if he said of a non-kosher animal or of a blemished one, “These are a burnt offering,” he has said nothing; “These are for a burnt offering,” they are sold and he brings a burnt offering with their money; one must say that he is flogged.

messages.text: It is taught in a baraita in accordance with the opinion of Rava:
messages.quote: even one who consecrates it to be sold and its money used for purchasing libations

messages.text: 7b

A vow offering differs from a gift offering in that if it dies prematurely, one is liable to replace the former but not the latter. The verse states: “Either a bull or a lamb that has anything too long or too short, you may offer it for a gift, and for a vow it shall not be accepted” (Leviticus 22:23).

verse.he: וְשׁוֹר וָשֶׂה שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט נְדָבָה תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתוֹ וּלְנֵדֶר לֹא יֵרָצֶה׃
verse.en: You may, however, present as a freewill offering an ox or a sheep with a limb extended or contracted; but it will not be accepted for a vow.

messages.text: The phrase “You may offer it for a gift” is referring to a blemished animal consecrated for Temple maintenance. And I have derived only that one may consecrate it in the manner of a gift; from where is it derived that one may consecrate it in the manner of a vow as well? The verse states: “You may offer it for a gift and for a vow.”

notes.he: לבעל מום לדמי קדשי בדק הבית דלמזבח לא אפשר לאקרוביה דהא כתיב (ויקרא כב) לא תתנו מהם וגו':
notes.en: “You may offer it for a gift”: a blemished animal, for the value of consecrated property for Temple maintenance; for the altar it cannot be offered, as it is written: “You shall not give of them” (Leviticus 22:22), etc.

notes.he: רבוי להתפיס בעל מום לבדק הבית:
notes.en: I have only: the inclusion permitting one to consecrate a blemished animal for Temple maintenance,

notes.he: על ידי נדבה כגון הרי זו לבדק הבית:
notes.en: only by way of a gift, for example: “This is for Temple maintenance.”

notes.he: שאם אמר הרי עלי בהמה לדמי בדק הבית שמצוה להפריש בעל מום תלמוד לומר ולנדר והכי נמי דריש נדבה תעשה אותו ולנדר כלומר וכן לנדר:
notes.en: From where a vow: that if he said, “It is incumbent on me [to give] an animal for the value of Temple maintenance,” it is a mitzva to set aside a blemished one? The verse states: “And for a vow.” He expounds it thus: “You may offer it for a gift, and for a vow,” that is, and likewise for a vow.

messages.text: One might have thought that one can consecrate blemished animals even as offerings to be sacrificed on the altar. Therefore, the verse states: “And for a vow it shall not be accepted.” This is referring to offerings sacrificed on the altar, for which acceptance is a relevant term.

notes.he: דשייכא בהו הרצאה:
notes.en: “It shall not be accepted”: these are offerings for the altar, to which acceptance applies.

messages.text: And I have derived only that one may not consecrate such an animal as a vow offering. From where is it derived that one may not do so as a gift offering? The verse states: “A gift…and for a vow it shall not be accepted.”

notes.he: דנדר סמוך ללא ירצה ומשמע דאם נדר הרי עלי עולה לא יביא בעלת מום:
notes.en: I have only a vow: since “vow” is adjacent to “it shall not be accepted,” and it implies that if he vowed, “It is incumbent on me [to bring] a burnt offering,” he may not bring a blemished animal.

notes.he: שאין רשאי לומר על בעלת מום הרי זו למזבח:
notes.en: From where a gift: that he may not say of a blemished animal, “This is for the altar”?

notes.he: ולנדר לא ירצה והכי מידריש נדבה אשר תעשה אותו או נדר לא ירצה:
notes.en: The verse states: “a gift… and for a vow it shall not be accepted.” It is expounded thus: “A gift that you make of it, or a vow: it shall not be accepted.”

messages.text: In employing the phrase “It shall not be accepted,” the verse is speaking of consecration that depends upon the acceptance of the animal’s body, i.e., consecration as an offering. Nevertheless, they may be consecrated for Temple maintenance.

notes.dh: רבי אמר לא ירצה בהרצאת גופו הכתוב מדבר
notes.he: שלא יקריבנו והיינו נמי קדשי מזבח כתנא קמא:
notes.en: Rabbi says: “It shall not be accepted”: the verse speaks of the acceptance of its body, that he may not sacrifice it; this too refers to offerings for the altar, like the first tanna.

messages.text: The opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is identical to the opinion of the first tanna. What is their dispute?
messages.quote: the verse is speaking of consecration that depends upon the acceptance of the animal’s body

messages.text: What, is it not that they disagree with regard to this, that the first tanna holds that even if one consecrates it to be sold and its money is used for purchasing libations, he is flogged as well; and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that in a case where there is acceptance of the animal’s body, the one who consecrated it is indeed flogged, but if one consecrates it to be sold and its money is used for purchasing libations, he is not flogged.
Learn from the baraita that the first tanna holds that consecration toward libations is equivalent to consecration as an offering, as Rava suggested above.
§ But why do I need the word “it,” in the phrase: “You may offer it”? What does this serve to exclude? It is required for that which is taught in a baraita:

notes.he: כלומר תינח כוליה קרא מוקמת לדרשא דקא דרשת האי נדבה ונדר:
notes.en: And he asks: Rather, what does “it” come for? That is, granted, the whole verse you establish for the exposition you expounded, this “gift” and “vow”;

notes.he: דכתיב (שם) נדבה תעשה אותו למה לי:
notes.en: but “it,” as written in “you may offer it for a gift,” why do I need it?

messages.text: When the verse states: “You may offer it for a gift,” this teaches that you may offer this blemished animal as a gift for Temple maintenance, but you may not offer an unblemished animal as a gift for Temple maintenance. From here the Sages said: One who consecrates unblemished animals for Temple maintenance transgresses a positive mitzva.

notes.he: בעל מום אתה מקדיש לבדק הבית כו':
notes.en: It: a blemished animal you may consecrate for Temple maintenance, etc.

notes.he: אהאי עשה דאמרינן ואי אתה מקדיש תמימים דהיינו לאו הבא מכלל עשה ועשה הוא:
notes.en: Transgresses a positive mitzva: this positive mitzva, that we say “but you may not consecrate unblemished ones,” which is a prohibition derived from a positive mitzva, and it counts as a positive mitzva.

notes.he: דלאו הבא מכלל עשה עשה:
notes.en: Transgresses a positive mitzva: for a prohibition derived from a positive mitzva is a positive mitzva.

messages.text: And from where is it derived that he has transgressed a prohibition as well? As it is stated at the beginning of that passage: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying [lemor]” (Leviticus 22:1). This teaches that every mitzva stated in the passage is considered a prohibition. This is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.
@Bar Kappara From where may it be inferred that every mitzva stated in the passage is considered a prohibition?
messages.quote: teaches that every mitzva stated in the passage is considered a prohibition

messages.text: As the verse states: “Lemor,” the term can be read as though it states: No [lo], an expression of prohibition, is stated [ne’emar] with regard to the subsequent matters.
messages.lead: Bar Kappara said to him that this is as it is written:

notes.he: כלומר בההיא פרשה:
notes.en: “No” is stated in the matters: that is, in that passage.

messages.text: The term should be understood to mean that God said to Moses: No [lo] shall you say [emor] to them these matters.
messages.lead: In the school of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi they say:

notes.he: כלומר הכי אמר הקב"ה לאו אמור להם לישראל דלאו איכא הכא דאי עברי אהך פרשה עוברין בלאו:
notes.en: “No” shall you say: that is, thus the Holy One, blessed be He, said: a prohibition is said to Israel; there is a prohibition here, so that if they transgress this passage they transgress a prohibition.

messages.text: § A baraita above (6b) stated that one who sacrifices a blemished animal on the altar transgresses the prohibition “You may not burn all of it,” and if he sacrificed part of it, he transgresses the prohibition “You may not burn part of it.” With regard to this it was stated:
he violates both the prohibition of “You may not burn all of it;” and the prohibition of “You may not burn part of it,” and he receives two sets of lashes.
messages.lead: In the case of one who brings up the limbs of blemished animals onto the altar,

notes.he: הנתחים כמשפט עולה:
notes.en: Limbs, etc.: the pieces, as is the law of a burnt offering.

notes.he: אימורין לוקה משום הקטרת כולו ומשום הקטרת מקצתו דיש בכלל כולו מקצתו. ואביי אמר אין לוקין על לאו שבכללות. על לאו שכולל בו ב' איסורין דכל הקטרת כולו וכל הקטרת מקצתו מחד לאו נפקא מלא תתנו:
notes.en: The limbs of blemished animals: the sacrificial portions. He is flogged for burning all of it and for burning part of it, since “all of it” includes “part of it.” And Abaye said: one is not flogged for a general prohibition, a prohibition that includes two prohibitions, for every burning of all of it and every burning of part of it come from one prohibition, from “you shall not give.”

messages.text: One is not flogged twice for violating a general prohibition. Since one verse serves as the source for both prohibitions, one is not flogged twice for its violation.
messages.quote: he violates both the prohibition of “You may not burn all of it;” and the prohibition of “You may not burn part of it”

notes.he: דהקטרת כולו ומקצתו מחד לאו נפקי ואשה לא תתנו מהם כדפרישית לעיל אבל לכולהו איכא לאו לכל חד וחד דהקדש נפיק מכל אשר בו מום לא תקריבו ודרשינן ליה לעיל (תמורה דף ו:) לא תקדישו ושחיטה מלא תקריבו אלה לה' דגבי עורת או שבור וזריקה מלא תקריבו דגבי מעוך וכתות (ויקרא כ״ב:כ״ב) והאי אין לוקין דאמר אביי אין לוקין תרתי קאמר אבל חדא איכא ואליבא למאן דאמר חדא מיהא לקי אלאו שבכללות בשילהי פרק שני דפסחים (מא:):
notes.en: For a general prohibition: for burning all of it and part of it come from one prohibition, “nor make an offering by fire of them,” as I explained above. But for all the others there is a prohibition for each one: consecration comes from “whatever has a blemish, you shall not offer,” which we expounded above (Temurah 6b) as “you shall not consecrate”; slaughter from “you shall not offer these unto the Lord,” said of the blind or broken; and sprinkling from “you shall not offer” said of the bruised or crushed [Leviticus 22:24]. The “one is not flogged” that Abaye said means one is not flogged twice, but once one is, according to the one who says that for a general prohibition one is at least flogged once, at the end of the second chapter of Pesaḥim (41b).

notes.dh: אביי אמר אין לוקין על לאו שבכללות
notes.he: פרש"י דהא אין לוקין דאמר אביי אין לוקין תרתי קאמר אבל חדא לקי ואליבא דמ"ד חדא מיהא לקי אלאו שבכללות בשילהי פ' כל שעה (פסחים דף מא:) לשון רש"י וכן מוכח הסוגיא:
notes.en: Abaye said: one is not flogged for a general prohibition: Rashi explained that the “one is not flogged” that Abaye said means one is not flogged twice, but once one is, according to the one who says that for a general prohibition one is at least flogged once, at the end of the chapter Kol Sha’a (Pesaḥim 41b). This is Rashi’s wording, and so the discussion proves.

messages.text: One who consecrates blemished animals for sacrifice on the altar violates five separate categories of prohibition.
messages.lead: The Gemara raises an objection from the Tosefta (1:10):

notes.he: וחשיב להו להני תרי בתרי:
notes.en: For five prohibitions: and it counts these two as two.

messages.text: The aforementioned baraita enumerated these and included both the prohibition “You may not burn all of it” and the prohibition “You may not burn part of it,” indicating that one is flogged for transgressing each of these prohibitions. This is apparently a conclusive refutation of the opinion of Abaye.
messages.quote: One is not flogged twice for violating a general prohibition

messages.text: The baraita is teaching the halakha with regard to different men, one of whom burned an entire animal on the altar, and one of whom burned only part of it. One person cannot be liable for both prohibitions.
messages.quote: violates five separate categories of prohibition

notes.he: דלאו בהכי עסקינן דאי עבדינהו לתרוייהו לילקי תרי אלא מילי מילי קתני שאם הקטיר כולו עובר משום בל תקטירו כולו או אם אדם אחד מקטיר מקצתו לוקה משום מקצתו אבל אי מקטיר חד לכולהו לא לקי אלא משום כולו:
notes.en: It teaches about men: we are not dealing with a case where, if one person did both, he is flogged twice; rather it teaches each matter separately: if he burned all of it he transgresses “you shall not burn all of it,” or if one person burns part of it he is flogged for “part of it.” But if one person does both, he is flogged only for “all of it.”

notes.he: אם הם חמשה אחד מקדיש ואחד שוחט ואחד מקטיר לוקה כל אחד:
notes.en: It teaches about men: if there are five, one consecrates, one slaughters and one burns, each one is flogged.

messages.text: If it is teaching the halakha of different men, why does it say: Violates, in the third person singular? It should have stated: Violate, in the plural.
Rather, it is obvious that the baraita is referring to one man, and this is apparently a conclusive refutation of the opinion of Abaye.

From the list of five prohibitions, remove that of burning part of the offering, and insert the collection of the blood, which means that there is only one prohibition for burning the offering, and the number of prohibitions still remains at five.

notes.he: או כולו או מקצתו ועייל קבלת הדם דנפקא מלא תקריבו דמיד בן נכר:
notes.en: Remove one of them, either “all of it” or “part of it,” and insert collection of the blood, which comes from “you shall not offer” in “neither from the hand of a foreigner.”

messages.text: With regard to the collection of the blood, Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, is of the opinion that one transgresses that prohibition, but the first tanna is not of that opinion. How, then, can Abaye contradict the first tanna?
messages.quote: and insert the collection of the blood

notes.dh: וקפריך קבלת הדם לתנא קמא לית ליה
notes.he: וקחשיב ה':
notes.en: And he challenges: the first tanna does not hold of collection of the blood, yet he counts five.

messages.text: It is difficult.
The Gemara presents an alternative version of the previous point.

But from the fact that the latter clause of the baraita is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, it may be inferred that the first clause is in accordance with the opinion of the Rabbis.

notes.he: כלומר רישא רבנן היא דלא מחייבי אקבלת הדם ואפילו הכי קא חשיב ה' וקשיא לאביי:
notes.en: The first clause is the Rabbis: that is, the first clause follows the Rabbis, who do not hold one liable for collection of the blood, and even so it counts five; and this is difficult for Abaye.

messages.text: ✖ The refutation of the opinion of Abaye is indeed a conclusive refutation.
Mishna
The priests substitute for their own offerings and Israelites substitute for their own offerings.

notes.he: קרבנות שהפריש הכהן לעצמו אם המיר בהן נתפסים בתמורה:
notes.en: Mishna. The priests substitute for their own: offerings that a priest set aside for himself; if he substituted for them, the substitutes are caught up [in sanctity].

notes.he: וישראל ממירין בשלהן:
notes.en: Mishna. The priests substitute for their own offerings, and Israelites substitute for their own.

messages.text: The priests substitute neither for a sin offering, nor for a guilt offering, nor for a firstborn offering that they received from an Israelite, as those animals are not their property, and one does not substitute an animal that is not his.

notes.he: שנתן לו ישראל שיקריבנו לו אם המיר בו הכהן אינו עושה תמורה על ידו דהא אין לו חלק בו אלא משעת הקטרת אימורין ואילך וזכה בבשר ואמר בברייתא בהאי פירקא אין אדם מתפיס בדבר שאינו שלו:
notes.en: Neither for a sin offering nor for a guilt offering: that an Israelite gave him to sacrifice on his behalf. If the priest substituted for it, he does not effect a substitute through it, since he has no share in it until the sacrificial portions have been burned, when he acquires the meat. And a baraita in this chapter says: a person cannot consecrate something that is not his.

notes.he: שנתן לו ישראל וטעמא מפרש הכא במשנה גופה:
notes.en: Nor for a firstborn: that an Israelite gave him; the reason is explained here in the mishna itself.

notes.he: אין הכהנים ממירין לא בחטאת ולא באשם של ישראל:
notes.en: Priests do not substitute for the sin offering or the guilt offering of an Israelite.

messages.text: For what reason can priests not substitute for a firstborn offering that they received from an Israelite? Does it not belong to them?

notes.he: הכהנים ממירין בבכור והלא כולו שלהן הוא ומחיים הוא נותנו לו ואין הישראל מתכפר בו:
notes.en: For what reason can priests not substitute for a firstborn? Isn’t it entirely theirs? [The Israelite] gives it to him while it is alive, and the Israelite does not achieve atonement through it.

messages.text: @Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri A sin offering and a guilt offering are a gift to the priest, and the firstborn offering is likewise a gift to the priest. Just as in the cases of a sin offering and a guilt offering, priests that receive one of them from an Israelite cannot substitute for it, so too with regard to a firstborn offering, priests that receive it from an Israelite cannot substitute for it.

notes.dh: כשם שאין הכהנים ממירין בחטאת ואשם
notes.he: דהא ודאי פשיטא לן דאינו זוכה בהן אלא מהקטרת אימורין ואילך:
notes.en: Just as priests do not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering: for it is certainly obvious to us that he acquires them only once the sacrificial portions have been burned.

messages.text: What is this comparison for him? If a priest does not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering, which priests do not acquire during the animals’ lifetimes, will you say the same with regard to a firstborn, which priests do acquire during the animal’s lifetime?
messages.quote: Just as in the cases of a sin offering and a guilt offering

notes.dh: מה לי אינו ממיר בחטאת ואשם
notes.he: כלומר דין הוא שאין כהנים ממירין בחטאת ואשם כו':
notes.en: What is it to me if he does not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering: that is, it is logical that priests do not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering, etc.

notes.he: ואם תאמר ואי זכין בהן בחייהן היכי מימר למאן דאמר בגמרא בתר מתכפר אזלינן ויש לומר דר"ל אף בתר מתכפר ולאו לאפוקי בעלים אתי:
notes.en: Which they do not acquire during their lifetimes: And if you ask: even if they did acquire them during their lifetimes, how could they substitute, according to the one in the Gemara who says that we follow the one who achieves atonement? One can answer that he means [we follow] the one who achieves atonement as well, and does not come to exclude the owners.

messages.text: @Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri But isn’t it already stated: “Then both it and its substitute shall be sacred” (Leviticus 27:10), which juxtaposes the consecration of the consecrated animal with that of its non-sacred substitute? Where is the consecrated animal imbued with sanctity? It is in the house of the owner. So too, the substitute animal is consecrated in the house of the owner. Therefore, the priest cannot substitute for the firstborn that he received because he is not the owner that initially consecrated it.

verse.he: לֹא יַחֲלִיפֶנּוּ וְלֹא־יָמִיר אֹתוֹ טוֹב בְּרָע אוֹ־רַע בְּטוֹב וְאִם־הָמֵר יָמִיר בְּהֵמָה בִּבְהֵמָה וְהָיָה־הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ׃
verse.en: One may not exchange or substitute another for it, either good for bad, or bad for good; if one does substitute one animal for another, the thing vowed and its substitute shall both be holy.

notes.he: מקיש התמורה להקדש עצמו היכן קדושה חלה על ההקדש בבית הבעלים אף תמורה לא תחול אלא בבית הבעלים אבל בבית כהן לא חיילא לגמרי הלכך אין כהן ממיר בבכור אבל ישראל אם המיר בו נתפס בקדושה שהרי ברשותו חלה קדושה על הבכור:
notes.en: It and its substitute: it juxtaposes the substitute to the consecrated animal itself. Where does sanctity take hold of the consecrated animal? In the owner’s house. So too a substitute takes effect only in the owner’s house; in the priest’s house it does not fully take effect. Therefore a priest does not substitute for a firstborn, but an Israelite, if he substituted for it, it is caught up in sanctity, for the sanctity of the firstborn took hold in his domain.

notes.he: והיה הוא ותמורתו יהיה קדש היינו קדושת של מימר שחלה עליו בבית הבעלים אף כל תמורה בבית הבעלים וכיון שבא ליד כהן יצא מבית בעלים הילכך אין ממירין:
notes.en: “Then both it and its substitute shall be sacred”: that is, the sanctity of the substituted animal took hold of it in the owner’s house; so too every substitution is in the owner’s house. Once it has come into the priest’s hand it has left the owner’s house; therefore they do not substitute.

messages.text: Gemara
We learned in a mishna elsewhere (Ma’aser Sheni 1:2):

With regard to a firstborn offering, one may sell it if it is unblemished only while it is still alive, as after it is slaughtered outside the Temple one may not derive benefit from it, and if it was offered in the Temple, one may not sell sacrificial meat. And if it is blemished, one may sell it while it is alive or after it has been slaughtered. And a priest can betroth a woman with it, as it is his property.

notes.he: השתא משמע בין בזמן המקדש בין בזמן הזה והכי משמע אם בית המקדש קיים מוכרין אותו כהן לכהן חי ואותו כהן יקריבנו אבל שחוט לא דבזיון קדשים הוא דלאו אורח ארעא לעשות סחורה בדבר שקרב ממנו למזבח ואי בזמן הזה הוא מוכרין אותו תמים חי בין כהן לכהן בין כהן לישראל והלוקח ימתין עד שיפול בו מום ויאכלנו דבכור בזמן הזה משנפל בו מום אין בו אלא איסור גזל שגזל את הכהן ואם מכרו כהן או נתנו לו מותר לאוכלו וכדאמרינן בבכורות [בפ' כל פסולי המוקדשין] (דף לב:) גבי בכור בעל מום (כל פסולי המוקדשין) ב"ה מתירין ואפי' עובד כוכבים מותר לאכול הימנו אבל בתם שחוט בזמן הזה ליכא:
notes.en: Gemara. They sell it unblemished and alive: as it stands this implies both when the Temple stands and in the present, and it means: if the Temple stands, they sell it alive from priest to priest, and that priest sacrifices it; but slaughtered, no, for that is a disgrace to consecrated items, as it is not proper to trade in something from which part is offered on the altar. And if in the present, they sell it unblemished and alive, whether from priest to priest or from priest to Israelite, and the buyer waits until a blemish befalls it and eats it. For a firstborn in the present, once a blemish befalls it, carries only the prohibition of robbery, of robbing the priest; if a priest sold it or gave it to him, it is permitted to eat it, as we say in Bekhorot, chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (32b), regarding a blemished firstborn: Beit Hillel permit, and even a gentile may eat of it. But an unblemished slaughtered one does not exist in the present.

notes.he: כהן את האשה דממוניה הוא:
notes.en: And one betroths with it: a priest betroths a woman with it, for it is his property.

notes.he: הכהנים תמים חי ובעל מום חי ושחוט ומקדש בו את האשה דממונן הוי:
notes.en: Gemara. A firstborn, they sell it: the priests, unblemished and alive, and blemished, alive or slaughtered; and one betroths a woman with it, for it is their property.

messages.text: They taught this halakha only with regard to the present, when there is no Temple, since the priest has the ability to acquire the firstborn offering. But when the Temple is standing, since the unblemished firstborn animal stands for sacrifice, one may not sell it unblemished while it is alive.
messages.quote: one may sell it if it is unblemished only while it is still alive

notes.he: דכהן יכול למוכרו חי:
notes.en: They taught only: that a priest can sell it alive

notes.he: דלא קאי להקרבה:
notes.en: only in the present: when it does not stand for sacrifice,

notes.he: מחיים דבזמן הזה נמי הוו הבכורות לכהנים:
notes.en: and the priest has acquisition in it: during its lifetime, for in the present too firstborns belong to the priests.

notes.he: דלית לכהן זכייה בגויה אלא מהקטרת אימורין ואילך:
notes.en: They do not sell it unblemished and alive: for the priest acquires it only once the sacrificial portions have been burned.

notes.he: וא"ת האמר פרק שור שנגח הפרה (ב"ק דף נג:) שור ושור פסולי המוקדשין שנגחו אביי אמר חצי נזק ומוקי לה במועד אבל שור של פסולי המוקדשין פטור אלמא לאו רעהו קרינא ביה וקאמר התם נמי דשור של הדיוט שנגח שור של פסולי המוקדשין חייב אלמא משמע דקרינא ביה רעהו וצריך לומר דקמייתא מיירי בבכור דלא מצי פריק וברייתא בשאר קדשים דפריק להו במומן והתם בזמן הזה איירי שהרי האמוראים דאיירי התם עלה לא הוו בזמן הבית ואפילו הכי קאמר התם דלאו ממונו הוא ואם כן קשה דהכא אמר דממונו הוא בזמן הזה וצריך לומר דהכא אתייא כרבי יוסי הגלילי וההיא דהתם כרבנן ואע"ג דבפ' קמא דב"ק (דף יב: ושם ד"ה ואם) אמר [ולשני] הא כרבי יוסי [והא כרבנן] צ"ל דלפי זה לא מיתוקמא ההיא סוגיא דפרק הפרה:
notes.en: They taught this only in the present: And if you ask: in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ et HaPara (Bava Kamma 53b), regarding “an ox and an ox of disqualified consecrated animals that gored,” Abaye said half damages and established it with a forewarned ox, but an ox of disqualified consecrated animals [that gored] is exempt; evidently “his fellow’s” does not apply to it. And it says there too that an ordinary person’s ox that gored an ox of disqualified consecrated animals is liable, implying that “his fellow’s” does apply. One must say that the first case speaks of a firstborn, which cannot be redeemed, and the baraita of other consecrated animals, which are redeemed on account of their blemish. And there it speaks of the present, for the Amoraim discussing it there did not live in Temple times, and even so it says there that it is not his property. If so, it is difficult, since here it says that in the present it is his property. One must say that here follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and there follows the Rabbis. And although in the first chapter of Bava Kamma (12b) it says [let him answer:] this follows Rabbi Yosei and this the Rabbis, one must say that according to this, that discussion in the chapter HaPara cannot be explained this way.

notes.dh: הואיל ואית ליה לכהן זכיה בגויה
notes.he: דכיון דאין מזבח הוי כולו דכהן:
notes.en: Since the priest has acquisition in it: for since there is no altar, it is entirely the priest’s.

messages.text: The mishna teaches that one may sell an unblemished firstborn offering while it is alive. One can infer that while it is alive, yes, one may sell it, but once it has been slaughtered, one may not sell it.
messages.quote: But when the Temple is standing

notes.dh: אי בזמן הזה מי איכא תם שחוט
notes.he: הא אין שוחטין את הבכור בזמן הזה אלא במומו כדתנן בבכורות מעשה בזכר של רחלים זקן וכו':
notes.en: If in the present, is there an unblemished slaughtered one? But one does not slaughter a firstborn in the present except on account of its blemish, as we learned in Bekhorot: “It happened with an old male ram,” etc.

messages.text: When is this the halakha? If we say that this mishna is speaking in the present, is there an unblemished, slaughtered, firstborn offering? Offerings are not slaughtered in the present day. Rather, it is obvious that the mishna is speaking of the time when the Temple is standing. And yet, the mishna still teaches that one may sell an unblemished firstborn offering while it is alive, which contradicts the statement of Rav Naḥman.

notes.he: הא הוי קדשים בחוץ:
notes.en: Is there an unblemished slaughtered one? That would be a consecrated animal [slaughtered] outside [the Temple].

messages.text: No; actually the mishna is referring to the halakha in the present. I disagree with the above inference. Does the mishna explicitly teach: One may sell an unblemished firstborn offering while it is alive, yes, but once it has been slaughtered, no?

notes.he: דמשמע מינה דלאו בזמן הזה דבזמן הזה ליכא תם שחוט:
notes.en: Does it teach “slaughtered, no”: which would imply that it is not in the present, since in the present there is no unblemished slaughtered one?

notes.he: ודקא קשיא לך מי איכא תם שחוט מי קתני בפירוש בברייתא אבל תם שחוט לא לא תני הכי אלא היא גופא קמ"ל. דמוכרין אותו תמים חי ובזמן הזה:
notes.en: No, actually in the present. As for your difficulty, “Is there an unblemished slaughtered one?”: does it teach explicitly, “but unblemished and slaughtered, no”? It does not teach that; rather it teaches us this itself: that they sell it unblemished and alive, and in the present.

messages.text: The mishna does not mean to rule out selling a slaughtered animal; rather, it is coming to teach us the matter itself, that even in the present, one may sell it unblemished while it is alive.

notes.he: כלומר מאי דקתני בברייתא גופה איצטריך לאשמועינן דמוכרין אותו תמים חי דס"ד דלית בהו זכייה עד שיפול בו מום ולאו משום דתידוק מינה שחוט לא דהא בזמן הזה קמיירי ובזמן הזה ליכא תם שחוט:
notes.en: It comes to teach us this itself: that is, what is taught [in the mishna] itself was needed to teach us that they sell it unblemished and alive, since it might enter your mind that they have no acquisition in them until a blemish befalls it; it is not so that you should infer from it “slaughtered, no,” for it deals with the present, and in the present there is no unblemished slaughtered one.

messages.text: Continued on 8a: Rava raises another objection to Rav Naḥman, from a baraita on the firstborn: “You shall not redeem”, but it may be sold.
